questions.q: What are the three mathematical pillars of ML in this lesson?
options: Linear algebra, calculus and probability & statistics
Algebra, graph theory and number theory
questions.explain: Data and parameters are vectors and matrices; training needs derivatives; loss functions come from probability.

questions.q: What do the symbols in θ_new = θ_old − α∇J(θ) mean?
options: θ is a parameter vector, ∇J the gradient of the cost, α a scalar learning rate
θ is a scalar, α a vector
questions.explain: It's the gradient descent update.

questions.q: Why is calculus needed for training?
options: The derivative of the error tells you which direction to adjust each parameter
questions.explain: It is the mechanism of learning.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say math matters even if .fit() runs without it?
options: When training diverges, loss becomes NaN or a model won't learn, the math is the only way through
questions.explain: It also helps you read papers' notation.

questions.q: A dataset has n examples with d features each. What is its matrix shape?
options: d × n, one row per example
n × d, one row per example
questions.explain: Each row is an example vector and each column a feature.

questions.q: What does 'rows first, columns second' mean for a 3 × 2 matrix?
questions.explain: Entry a_ij is row i, column j.

questions.q: What is a tensor?
options: A generalization with more axes, like a batch of images stacked into 3D/4D
questions.explain: Level 1 sticks to scalars, vectors and matrices.

questions.q: What does the identity matrix do when you multiply by it?
questions.explain: It has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere.

questions.q: What is the dot product of [1,2,3] and [4,5,6]?
What does a dot product of 0 tell you about two vectors?
questions.explain: u·v = ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ, which is 0 at 90°.

questions.q: What is the Euclidean norm of [3, 4]?
What does a linear model's prediction ŷ = w·x correspond to?
options: A dot product of weights and features
questions.explain: Every linear layer in a neural network is a stack of dot products; cosine similarity compares embeddings.

questions.q: For AB to be defined with A (m×n) and B (p×q), what must hold?
options: n = p, and the result is m × q
questions.explain: The inner dimensions must match.

questions.q: Is matrix multiplication commutative?
questions.explain: Check it yourself in the exercise.

questions.q: What does ŷ = Xw compute?
questions.explain: X is n × d and w is d × 1.

questions.q: What is training a model, in terms of the cost function J(θ)?
options: Finding the input θ that minimizes J
questions.explain: J takes parameters as input and outputs how wrong the model is.

questions.q: Why can gradient descent reliably find the minimum of a linear regression cost?
options: It is a quadratic 'bowl' with one unique minimum
questions.explain: A parabola with a > 0 opens upward with a single minimum.

questions.q: What is a composite function?
options: One function plugged into another, h(x) = f(g(x))
questions.explain: A neural network is a long chain of compositions, differentiated by the chain rule.

questions.q: What is the average rate of change between x₁ and x₂?
options: The slope of the secant line: (f(x₂) − f(x₁)) / (x₂ − x₁)
questions.explain: Shrinking the gap to zero gives the instantaneous rate of change.

questions.q: What is the derivative geometrically?
options: The slope of the tangent line at a point
questions.explain: It's the instantaneous rate of change.

questions.q: What is f'(x) for f(x) = x² derived from first principles?
questions.explain: Expanding (x+h)² and cancelling h gives lim (2x + h) = 2x.

questions.q: Using h = 0.001 at x = 3 for f(x) = x², the finite-difference estimate is?
Where f'(x) = 0, what does the tangent look like and why does it matter for ML?
options: It is flat, marking a candidate minimum, maximum or saddle; minima of the cost occur there
questions.explain: That's why derivatives matter for training.

questions.q: What is d/dx[x³] by the power rule?
questions.explain: n·x^(n−1) with n = 3.

questions.q: What is the derivative of f(x) = 3x² + 4x + 7?
questions.explain: The sum rule works term by term; the constant's derivative is 0.

questions.q: For h(x) = (3x + 1)², what is h'(x) by the chain rule?
questions.explain: Outer derivative 2(3x+1) times inner derivative 3, which equals 18x + 6.

questions.q: Why is the chain rule the most important rule for ML?
options: It is the mathematical mechanism behind backpropagation, since a network is a composition of functions
questions.explain: Backpropagation is covered in Level 3.

questions.q: What is ∂f/∂x for f(x,y) = x²y + 3y² + 5x?
questions.explain: Treat y as a constant: x²y gives 2xy, 3y² gives 0, and 5x gives 5.

questions.q: What is the gradient ∇f?
options: A vector of all partial derivatives
questions.explain: For the example, ∇f = [2xy + 5, x² + 6y].

questions.q: What does ∇f(2, 1) equal for that function?
Which direction does −∇f point?
options: The direction of steepest decrease, which is why gradient descent steps along it
questions.explain: It's the locally best direction to reduce the cost.

questions.q: What cost function does the lesson use for linear regression?
options: Mean squared error J(w,b) = (1/n) Σ (wx_i + b − y_i)²
questions.explain: A function of two variables, w and b.

questions.q: What is ∂J/∂b for that cost?
questions.explain: By the chain rule ∂u_i/∂b = 1; for w it's x_i.

questions.q: Why does the cost have a single global minimum?
options: It is quadratic in (w, b), a bowl shape
questions.explain: Set both partial derivatives to zero to solve.

questions.q: What does the closed-form b* equal?
questions.explain: With w* = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)/Σ(x−x̄)².

questions.q: For J(w,b) = (w−3)² + (b+2)² + wb, what is ∂J/∂w?
questions.explain: The (b+2)² term has no w, and wb differentiates to b.

questions.q: What is ∇J(1, 1)?
What is J(1, 1)?
Why verify a hand-derived gradient numerically in NumPy?
options: To cross-check the hand work against finite differences
questions.explain: Both a symbolic formula and a numerical check are compared.

questions.q: What is the gradient descent update?
questions.explain: α is the learning rate.

questions.q: For J(θ) = (θ−3)² + 2, starting at 0 with α = 0.3, what is θ₁?
By what factor does the distance to the minimum shrink each step in that example?
questions.explain: The contraction factor is |1 − 2α|.

questions.q: What happens for that quadratic when α > 1?
questions.explain: Too small a rate is slow; α near 0.5 converges in one step here.

questions.q: What is the multivariable chain rule for z = f(x,y) with x(t), y(t)?
questions.explain: Each path from t to z contributes a term.

questions.q: For z = x²y, x = t², y = 3t, what is dz/dt?
questions.explain: z = 3t⁵ by substitution, so dz/dt = 15t⁴.

questions.q: Why does this rule matter for ML?
options: It makes backpropagation possible: each layer contributes a gradient term combined via dot products along the graph
questions.explain: Neural networks compose many multivariable functions.

questions.q: What does the numeric check at t = 2 expect?
What shape is the Jacobian of f: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ?
questions.explain: Row i is ∇f_i transposed: all the per-output gradients stacked.

questions.q: What is the Jacobian of f(x,y) = (x²y, x + y²) at (1, 2)?
What does the Hessian contain?
options: Second partial derivatives of a scalar function, describing local curvature
questions.explain: For smooth functions it is symmetric.

questions.q: All Hessian eigenvalues are positive at a critical point. What is it?
questions.explain: All negative means maximum; mixed signs means saddle.

questions.q: What is an eigenvector of a square matrix A?
options: A nonzero v with Av = λv, which A only scales without changing its direction
questions.explain: λ is its eigenvalue.

questions.q: How are eigenvalues found?
options: By solving the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0
questions.explain: A − λI must be singular for a nonzero v to exist.

questions.q: What are the eigenvalues of A = [[4,1],[2,3]]?
Which property do symmetric matrices like covariance and Hessians have?
questions.explain: For PCA, eigenvectors of the covariance matrix are the principal directions.

questions.q: Which decomposition applies to any matrix, even non-square?
questions.explain: Eigendecomposition needs a square matrix.

questions.q: How do singular values relate to eigenvalues?
questions.explain: They're non-negative and sorted descending.

questions.q: For a symmetric A, eigendecomposition becomes?
questions.explain: Because V⁻¹ = Vᵀ when V is orthogonal.

questions.q: For A = diag(3, −2), what are the singular values?
questions.explain: AᵀA has eigenvalues 9 and 4, so σ = 3 and 2.

questions.q: What is P(A ∪ B) in general?
questions.explain: Inclusion–exclusion.

questions.q: For a fair die, A = even, B = ≥ 4. What is P(A | B)?
Are A and B independent there?
questions.explain: Independence needs P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B).

questions.q: What does 'naive' in naive Bayes mean?
options: The assumption that features are independent, often false but useful
questions.explain: It applies conditional probability and independence rules directly.

questions.q: What is E[X] for a fair die roll?
What is Var(X) for a fair die?
What does Var(aX + b) equal?
questions.explain: Shifting doesn't change spread; scaling by a scales variance by a².

questions.q: Is E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] true for dependent variables?
questions.explain: Linearity holds regardless of dependence.

questions.q: What is Bayes' theorem?
questions.explain: Posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence.

questions.q: A disease affects 1%; a test has a 99% true positive rate and 5% false positive rate. What is P(D | +)?
Why is the positive result only about 16.7% reliable?
options: The disease is rare, so false positives from the large healthy population dominate (base-rate fallacy)
questions.explain: Bayes' theorem corrects for the base rate.

questions.q: What does naive Bayes assume?
options: Features are conditionally independent given the class
questions.explain: So P(x|c) = ∏ P(x_i|c).

questions.q: What are the mean and variance of a Bernoulli(p)?
questions.explain: It models a single binary trial.

questions.q: What is P(X = 6) for 10 fair coin flips?
What are the Binomial mean and variance for n = 10, p = 0.5?
questions.explain: np and np(1−p).

questions.q: Why is the Gaussian so common in ML?
options: The Central Limit Theorem: sums of many independent effects tend toward it; Gaussian errors lead to MSE loss
questions.explain: Noise and weight initializations often assume it.

questions.q: What does the capstone estimate with gradient descent?
options: The heads probability p, by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli flips
questions.explain: The same strategy trains logistic regression.

questions.q: Why take logs of the likelihood?
options: It turns the product into a sum, which is much easier to differentiate
questions.explain: ℓ(p) = Σ[y ln p + (1−y) ln(1−p)].

questions.q: With 7 heads in 10 flips, what is the closed-form optimum p*?
questions.explain: n₁/n, the sample mean.

questions.q: For n₁ = 7, n₀ = 3 and α = 0.02, what is p₁ starting from p = 0.5?
What is backpropagation, per the lesson?
options: The multivariable chain rule applied layer by layer, reusing intermediate results
A separate algorithm unrelated to calculus
questions.explain: The forward pass caches every intermediate value so none is recomputed.

questions.q: For a = σ(z), what is ∂a/∂z?
questions.explain: The sigmoid derivative.

questions.q: For x = 2, y = 1, w = 0.5, b = 0, what are z and a?
What is the shared upstream term δ?
options: ∂L/∂z = 2(a − y)a(1 − a), reused for both ∂L/∂w (× x) and ∂L/∂b
questions.explain: That reuse is the 'backward propagation of error'.

questions.q: What is the gradient of MSE with respect to a single prediction?
questions.explain: Power rule plus linearity under the sum.

questions.q: What does composing BCE with a sigmoid give for ∂L/∂z_i?
options: (1/n)(ŷ_i − y_i), because the ŷ(1−ŷ) terms cancel
questions.explain: It's why frameworks fuse sigmoid + BCE into one stable operation.

questions.q: For ŷ = [0.8, 0.3] and y = [1, 0], what is the MSE?
What is BCE the per-example, averaged form of?
options: The negative log-likelihood from the Bernoulli model
questions.explain: It's the same strategy as Level 2's capstone.

questions.q: What does momentum use instead of the raw gradient?
options: An exponentially decaying running average of past gradients
questions.explain: Like a ball rolling downhill, it smooths oscillations.

questions.q: For J(θ) = (θ−3)² + 2, θ₀ = 0, α = 0.3, β = 0.9, what is θ₁ with momentum?
What two running averages does Adam track?
options: The gradient mean (first moment) and the squared-gradient average (second moment)
questions.explain: It uses both to adapt step size per parameter.

questions.q: Why does Adam bias-correct m_t and v_t?
options: Because they start at zero, early estimates are biased toward zero
questions.explain: m̂ = m/(1−β₁ᵗ) and v̂ = v/(1−β₂ᵗ).

questions.q: What is the regularized objective?
questions.explain: λ controls the penalty strength.

questions.q: Why is L2 called weight decay?
options: Each step shrinks w multiplicatively by (1 − 2ηλ) before the data gradient
questions.explain: The gradient is ∇L + 2λw.

questions.q: Why does L1 give sparsity?
options: It subtracts a constant amount from each weight regardless of magnitude, and its diamond contour has corners on the axes
questions.explain: L2 shrinks smoothly but rarely to exactly zero.

questions.q: For w = 3, L = (w−1)², λ = 0.5, η = 0.1, what is the L2 step result?
What does MLE choose?
options: Parameters that make the observed data most probable under an assumed distribution
The mean of the data always
questions.explain: Maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the negative log-likelihood.

questions.q: Why maximize the log-likelihood instead of the likelihood?
options: Products underflow numerically; log is monotonic so the maximizer is unchanged
questions.explain: It also turns products into sums.

questions.q: MSE is the MLE under which noise model?
questions.explain: Dropping constants, minimizing −ℓ is minimizing Σ(y − f)².

questions.q: Binary cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of which model?
What does softmax do?
options: Turns raw logits into a probability distribution
questions.explain: softmax(z)_i = e^{z_i} / Σ e^{z_j}.

questions.q: What is the combined gradient of softmax + cross-entropy with respect to the logits?
questions.explain: The cleanest gradient in deep learning.

questions.q: For logits (2.0, 1.0, 0.1) and true class 0, which is the approximate loss?
Why subtract max(z) in a softmax implementation?
options: Numerical stability, avoiding overflow in exp
questions.explain: It doesn't change the result.

questions.q: What does reverse-mode autodiff do?
options: A forward pass computes node values, then a backward pass propagates ∂L/∂v from the output using the chain rule
questions.explain: It is what backprop is.

questions.q: When is reverse mode cheaper than forward mode?
options: With many inputs and one scalar output, like millions of weights and a loss
With few inputs and many outputs
questions.explain: One backward pass regardless of parameter count.

questions.q: For f = (x+y)(xy) at x = 2, y = 3, what is ∂f/∂x?
Why are gradients summed at nodes with several consumers?
options: x contributes through multiple paths; the multivariable chain rule sums over paths
questions.explain: x feeds both a and b.

questions.q: What does batch normalization do?
options: Standardizes activations over a mini-batch, then applies a learnable rescale y = γx̂ + β
questions.explain: It stabilizes training.

questions.q: Why do γ and β exist?
options: They let the network undo the normalization if that's optimal
questions.explain: ε prevents division by zero.

questions.q: For batch (1, 2, 3), what are μ_B and σ_B²?
questions.explain: The population variance is (1 + 0 + 1)/3.

questions.q: Why is the backward pass easy to get wrong?
options: μ_B and σ_B² depend on every x_i in the batch, so gradients must account for that shared dependency
questions.explain: It's the sum-over-paths rule applied to the two shared nodes.

questions.q: What is the log-sum-exp trick for softmax?
options: Subtract max(z) before exponentiating: mathematically identical but safe from overflow
questions.explain: Every exponent becomes ≤ 0, so each term is in (0, 1].

questions.q: Why not compute log(softmax(z)) in two steps?
options: A probability can underflow to exactly 0, giving log(0); fuse as z_k − logsumexp(z)
questions.explain: The fused form never materializes a zero probability.

questions.q: What is catastrophic cancellation?
options: Subtracting two nearly equal large floats destroys precision, e.g. the one-pass variance going negative
questions.explain: The two-pass formula Σ(x − x̄)²/n is more stable.

questions.q: For logits (1000, 1001, 999), what does the stable softmax give approximately?
questions.explain: With c = 1001 the exponents are (−1, 0, −2); the naive version overflows to NaN.

questions.q: What is the combined gradient ∂L/∂z₂ for sigmoid output with BCE loss?
How does the gradient flow into the hidden layer?
options: δ₁ = δ₂ w₂ ⊙ a₁(1 − a₁): through w₂, then through the sigmoid derivative
questions.explain: Then ∂L/∂W₁ = δ₁ xᵀ and ∂L/∂b₁ = δ₁.

questions.q: How is the hand derivation verified?
questions.explain: The capstone combines backprop, loss derivatives and numeric checks.

questions.q: What is true of every local minimum of a convex function?
questions.explain: There are no traps.

questions.q: How do you test a twice-differentiable function in n dimensions for convexity?
options: Its Hessian is positive semi-definite everywhere (all eigenvalues ≥ 0)
questions.explain: This connects to the eigenvalue module.

questions.q: Why does gradient descent find the global optimum for linear and logistic regression but not neural networks?
options: Their losses are convex in the weights; network loss landscapes are non-convex
questions.explain: Networks can get stuck in local minima or saddle points.

questions.q: f(w₁,w₂) = w₁² + 2w₂² − w₁w₂ has Hessian eigenvalues of about 1.586 and 4.414. What does that imply?
questions.explain: Both are positive, so the Hessian is positive definite.

questions.q: What condition holds at a constrained optimum with g(x) = 0?
questions.explain: Otherwise you could slide along the constraint and decrease f.

questions.q: Minimizing x² + y² subject to x + y = 1 gives what point and value?
questions.explain: x = y = λ/2 with λ = 1.

questions.q: What does complementary slackness say about an inequality constraint?
options: Either the constraint is active (h = 0) or its multiplier μ is zero
questions.explain: The KKT condition μ·h(x) = 0.

questions.q: How does this relate to SVM support vectors?
options: Only points on the margin (active constraints) get nonzero μ
questions.explain: That's their 'support'.

questions.q: What does entropy H(p) measure?
options: The average surprise of a distribution, maximal for the uniform distribution and 0 when all mass is on one outcome
questions.explain: −log p_i is the surprise of outcome i.

questions.q: What is D_KL(p‖q) in terms of cross-entropy?
questions.explain: It is always ≥ 0, with equality iff p = q.

questions.q: Why does minimizing cross-entropy equal minimizing KL divergence?
options: H(p) doesn't depend on the model
questions.explain: Training a classifier minimizes KL from the true label distribution to the prediction.
−log(0.7), with H(p) = 0 for a one-hot label.

questions.q: What is the gradient of the logistic loss with respect to w?
questions.explain: The same form as linear regression, with ŷ = σ(z) instead of identity.

questions.q: Why is the logistic loss convex?
options: Its Hessian XᵀSX with S = diag(ŷ(1−ŷ)) is positive semi-definite
questions.explain: ŷ(1 − ŷ) > 0 for all ŷ in (0, 1).

questions.q: What does convexity guarantee here?
options: Gradient descent finds the global optimum
questions.explain: The gradient there is (ŷ − y)x = (−0.5744, −1.1488).

questions.q: What does the kernel trick avoid?
options: Explicitly computing the high-dimensional feature map φ(x)
questions.explain: k(x,z) = φ(x)ᵀφ(z) computed in the original space.

questions.q: For x = (1,2), z = (3,1), what is the polynomial kernel (xᵀz)²?
questions.explain: (3 + 2)² = 25, matching the explicit feature-map dot product.

questions.q: What does the RBF kernel correspond to?
questions.explain: k = exp(−‖x−z‖² / 2σ²).

questions.q: What is Mercer's condition?
options: A valid kernel's Gram matrix must be positive semi-definite for every finite point set
questions.explain: It guarantees a valid φ exists.

questions.q: What does SVD A = UΣVᵀ guarantee?
options: It exists for any m × n matrix, with orthogonal U and V and non-negative singular values
It exists only for square matrices
questions.explain: Σ is diagonal with σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ 0.

questions.q: How are singular values related to AᵀA?
options: σ_i² are the eigenvalues of AᵀA, and the columns of V are its eigenvectors
σ_i are the eigenvalues of A
questions.explain: AᵀA and AAᵀ are symmetric PSD, so SVD always exists.

questions.q: What does the Eckart–Young theorem say?
options: Keeping the top k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation in Frobenius error
questions.explain: It underlies PCA and compression.

questions.q: What are the singular values of diag(3, −2)?
questions.explain: AᵀA has eigenvalues 9 and 4.

questions.q: What are the prior, likelihood and posterior?
options: The loss, the gradient and the step
Belief before data, the data's probability given θ, and the updated belief after data
questions.explain: The evidence p(D) is a normalizing constant.

questions.q: How does MAP differ from MLE?
options: MAP maximizes likelihood × prior (prior-informed); MLE ignores the prior
questions.explain: A Gaussian prior on weights adds an L2 penalty λ‖w‖².

questions.q: A Beta(1,1) prior and 7 heads in 10 flips give which posterior?
questions.explain: Posterior = Beta(α + k, β + n − k).

questions.q: What does 'conjugate' mean here?
options: The posterior is in the same family as the prior, with a simple update
questions.explain: Beta is conjugate to Bernoulli.

questions.q: What does Newton's method use that gradient descent doesn't?
options: The Hessian, modeling f locally as a quadratic and jumping to its minimum

questions.q: How many steps does Newton's method need for a truly quadratic f?
questions.explain: Near the optimum it converges quadratically for general convex f.

questions.q: Why is Newton's method rarely used directly in deep learning?
options: Computing and inverting the Hessian costs O(n³), infeasible for millions or billions of parameters
questions.explain: Practitioners use quasi-Newton methods like L-BFGS or Adam.

questions.q: For f(x) = x⁴ − 3x³ + 2 from x₀ = 3, what is the Newton step's x₁?
What is scaled dot-product attention?
questions.explain: It's a weighted average of the values.

questions.q: Why divide by √d_k?
options: Dot products have variance d_k; without scaling softmax saturates and gradients vanish
questions.explain: Dividing restores variance to about 1 regardless of dimension.

questions.q: What does row i, column j of QKᵀ represent?
options: qᵢ · kⱼ, how much query i attends to key j
questions.explain: Softmax is applied row-wise.

questions.q: In the worked example both keys score 1 with d_k = 4. What is the output?
questions.explain: A tie gives an even blend of v₁ and v₂.

questions.q: What do the normal equations give?
questions.explain: It requires XᵀX to be invertible.

questions.q: When do the normal equations fail or become unstable?
options: When features are collinear (XᵀX singular or ill-conditioned)
questions.explain: SVD handles near-zero singular values gracefully.

questions.q: For X = [[1,1],[1,2],[1,3]] and y = (2,3,5), what are the fitted bias and slope?
What are the three methods the capstone compares?
options: Normal equations, gradient descent and the SVD pseudoinverse
questions.explain: All three agree numerically.

questions.q: A model's loss becomes NaN during training with large logits. Which fix applies?
options: Use the log-sum-exp / subtract-max trick in softmax
questions.explain: Naive softmax overflows exp; subtracting the max is mathematically identical but safe.

questions.q: You need all n predictions of a linear model at once. Which expression?
options: ŷ = Xw with X (n × d) and w (d × 1)
questions.explain: Matrix-vector multiplication computes every prediction in one step.

questions.q: The gradient of a cost points in which direction, and which way does gradient descent step?
options: ∇J points steepest down; descent steps along ∇J
∇J points steepest up; descent steps along −∇J
questions.explain: θ ← θ − α∇J.

questions.q: You want the derivative of (3x + 1)². Which rule and result?
questions.explain: Outer derivative times the inner derivative.

questions.q: Why is a quick check of a hand-derived gradient with finite differences useful?
options: It cross-checks the analytic gradient numerically
questions.explain: The capstones verify every hand derivation numerically.

questions.q: A positive-definite Hessian at a critical point means what?
questions.explain: All eigenvalues positive means a minimum.

questions.q: Which matrix factorization applies to a non-square matrix?
questions.explain: SVD exists for any matrix.

questions.q: For a fair die, what are E[X] and Var(X)?
A disease affects 1% of people; a test has 99% sensitivity and 5% false positives. A positive result means roughly?
questions.explain: Bayes' theorem corrects for the rare base rate.

questions.q: Which loss is the MLE under Gaussian noise, and which under a Bernoulli model?
questions.explain: Negative log-likelihood under each model yields those losses.

questions.q: Why does a softmax + cross-entropy gradient simplify to p − y?
options: The p_i(δ_ij − p_j) terms cancel against −y_i/p_i
questions.explain: That is why frameworks fuse the two operations.

questions.q: Adam divides each step by √v̂. What does that provide?
questions.explain: Large consistent gradients get smaller steps; sparse small gradients get larger ones.

questions.q: What does L1 regularization tend to do that L2 does not?
options: Push many weights exactly to zero (sparsity)
questions.explain: Its diamond contour has corners on the axes.

questions.q: In reverse-mode autodiff, why are gradients summed at a node with two consumers?
options: The value contributes through multiple paths (multivariable chain rule)
questions.explain: For f = (x+y)(xy), x contributes via both a and b.

questions.q: Why can gradient descent be trusted to find the global optimum of logistic regression but not of a neural network?
options: Its loss is convex in the weights; network losses are non-convex
questions.explain: Convexity means every local minimum is global.

questions.q: You must minimize f subject to g(x) = 0. What do you set up?
options: A Lagrangian L = f − λg and solve its stationary points
questions.explain: ∇f = λ∇g at the constrained optimum.

questions.q: What does the RBF kernel let an SVM do?
